about.title: Los Angeles Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Close to four million people live in Los Angeles, and nearly all of them spend part of each day on property that belongs to someone else. Grocery stores, strip-mall parking lots, apartment courtyards, hotel lobbies, office towers, restaurants, gyms, and the sidewalks that stitch the city together are all places where a wet floor, a broken step, or poor lighting can send a person down hard. Under California premises liability law, the injured person generally has to show that the owner or operator knew about the hazard, or reasonably should have known, and failed to fix it or warn about it. That element, called notice, is often where a Los Angeles fall claim is won or lost. Two other rules matter here. Most claims must be filed within two years, but a fall on property controlled by the City of Los Angeles, Los Angeles County, or another public agency carries a much shorter government-claim window, often only six months. And because California follows pure comparative fault, being partly responsible reduces a recovery rather than erasing it. Photographs, incident reports, witness names, and a prompt request to preserve surveillance footage can make a real difference. LawProactive connects Los Angeles residents with an independent attorney, free, and network attorneys work on contingency.

whyChoose.title: Why Los Angeles Residents Use LawProactive After a Fall

items.title: Notice Is the Heart of the Case
items.desc: California requires proof the property owner knew or should have known about the hazard. An attorney familiar with Los Angeles businesses and landlords knows how to look for inspection logs, prior complaints, and maintenance records that establish that knowledge.

items.title: Video Disappears Fast
items.desc: Most Los Angeles retailers, apartment complexes, and parking structures record on loops that overwrite within days or weeks. Getting an attorney involved early means a written preservation demand can go out before the footage of your fall is gone.

items.title: Two Deadlines, Not One
items.desc: Private-property claims generally have two years, but a fall on city, county, school district, or transit property triggers a far shorter government-claim deadline. An independent attorney can sort out who controlled the property and which clock is running before time slips away.

items.question: I tripped on a lifted sidewalk in Los Angeles. Who is actually responsible?
items.answer: It depends on who controls that stretch of pavement, which in Los Angeles can be the City, a county agency, or in some situations the adjacent property owner. When a public entity is involved, California requires a formal government claim on a much shorter timeline than the usual two years, so it is important to act quickly. Photograph the exact location, note the cross streets, and get medical care right away so the record is clear.

items.question: The store manager says I should have been watching where I was walking. Does that end my claim?
items.answer: No. California uses pure comparative fault, which means a jury or adjuster assigns percentages of responsibility rather than deciding all or nothing. If you are found partly at fault, your recovery is reduced by that percentage, but it is not eliminated. The property owner still has to answer for a hazard they knew about or should have known about.

items.question: How do I get the surveillance footage of my fall before it is erased?
items.answer: Ask the business in writing, the same day if possible, to preserve all video from the time of your fall, and keep a copy of your request. Many systems in Los Angeles overwrite footage in a matter of days, so a preservation letter from an attorney carries extra weight and puts the owner on formal notice not to destroy evidence. In the meantime, take your own photos of the hazard, the lighting, and any missing warning signs.
